*** THE CONSUL CLAIM IS TESTED FOR THE FIRST TIME ***
column2: South African Government Gazette, via Gazettes.Africa - free, official, 54,441 South African gazettes
column3: *** OPEN QUESTION 2 HAS NAMED THIS TEST SINCE 8 SEPTEMBER AND NOBODY HAD RUN IT ***
column4: The family and several later records call Pablo Armando a Consul General. Open question 2 says the decisive document is the *** exequatur *** - the host state's formal recognition of a foreign consul, 'crisp, dated and decisive' - and that the archive 'has not tested the claim against any official list'.
column5: *** It has now, and the archive already used this source for estates without ever asking it this question. ***

column1: *** THE CONTROLS, BOTH OF WHICH PASS ***
column2: coverage and vocabulary, checked before any null was written
column3: *** COVERAGE 1910-2026. 'exequatur' RETURNS 644 DOCUMENTS WITH PRE-1950 HITS IN 1914, 1932, 1933 AND 1937. ***
column4: A null is worthless unless the corpus reaches the years and carries the words.
column5: *** So the South African gazettes of his lifetime ARE digitised and full-text searchable, and the consular vocabulary IS present in them. *** The gazette's own formula was found in the process: *** 'RECOGNITION GRANTED AS CONSUL-GENERAL', 'RECOGNITION GRANTED AS VICE-CONSUL', 'Withdrawal of the Recognition as Honorary Consul' *** - which is what such a notice looks like and what any future sweep should search for.

column1: *** AND THE RESULT: NOT ONE LERENA BEFORE 1951 ***
column2: the surname across every South African gazette on the site, all five result pages walked
column3: *** 35 SOUTH AFRICAN DOCUMENTS CARRY THE NAME. THE EARLIEST IS 1951. ***
column4: He reached Cape Town by 1908 and died there in 1950.
column5: *** The earliest is Government Gazette no. 4584 of 1951 - the estate notice this archive already holds, 'Robert Paul Lerena, RACEHORSE TRAINER, of Newlands'. *** Everything else is 1971 or later. *** So across the whole of his life in South Africa the name does not appear in the official gazette at all *** - and a consular recognition of any rank, honorary included, is exactly the thing that would have put it there.

column1: *** WHAT THIS IS NOT, AND IT IS NOT A CLOSED NULL ***
column2: the limits, written down before the finding is used
column3: *** THREE REASONS IT IS AN INDICATION RATHER THAN AN ANSWER ***
column4: It would be easy to read the above as settling question 2 in the negative.
column5: *** FIRST, THE SPELLINGS HAVE NOT BEEN SWEPT. *** This archive's own rule - a null on one spelling is a null on a letter, not on a family - applies with full force to 1910s-40s newsprint OCR. *** SERENA, LLERENA, LORENA, LARENA, LEVENA and LERINA have NOT been run against the gazette. *** SECOND, the site's country filter DOES NOT BIND: a search for Lerena with country=za returns Mozambique documents, and the South African subset had to be taken by filtering result links on their /akn/za prefix. *** THIRD, THE TWO DOCUMENTS THAT WOULD NAME THE ACTUAL ARGENTINE CONSULS ARE UNREAD *** - gazettes *** 2594 of 30 December 1938 *** and *** 4389 of 26 May 1950 *** both surface on a search for 'Argentine Republic' and consul, and both sit behind a Cloudflare bot check. *** This archive does not work around bot detection, so they are recorded as BLOCKED rather than searched. ***

column2: the honorary-consul reading, which open question 2 already prefers
column3: *** AN HONORARY CONSUL IS STILL GAZETTED ***
column4: The page's own best hypothesis is that he was an *** honorary *** consul - a resident merchant holding the post - which would explain a diplomat who bred horses and farmed ostriches, and would keep him out of the career foreign-service lists.
column5: *** That hypothesis does not survive this test as comfortably as it looks. *** The gazette publishes recognitions of *** honorary *** consuls explicitly - the phrase 'Withdrawal of the Recognition as Honorary Consul of Finland' appears in the same corpus - so an honorary appointment is NOT a way of being absent from the gazette. *** If the exequatur route holds up under the spellings, the claim will have to rest on something other than a South African recognition *** - an Argentine appointment never recognised locally, a courtesy title, or the passport being remembered a generation later as a post.
